bull.b: Royal Caribbean has rebuilt a highly profitable earnings base, with strong TTM revenue, margins and net income following the prior downturn. This scale supports reinvestment in ships, destinations and customer experiences while providing operating leverage if demand remains healthy over the next several quarters.

Record pricing, solid booking activity and rising ancillary purchases indicate customers are engaging across the full vacation platform, not only buying cabins. Expanding loyalty participation and digital adoption can support repeat demand, higher guest spend and more durable revenue per passenger over time.

Replacing floating-rate borrowings with long-dated senior notes should improve maturity planning and reduce exposure to future interest-rate volatility. Although total debt remains high, this refinancing action can make financing costs more predictable and support capital allocation through the medium term.

bear.b: Royal Caribbean has improved materially from peak leverage, but its debt burden remains substantial relative to equity. That structure leaves earnings and cash flow more sensitive to demand slowdowns, refinancing conditions and interest expense, limiting financial flexibility compared with less leveraged travel companies.

Strong operating cash generation is not currently translating into positive cash remaining after investment and working-capital needs. Negative TTM free cash flow constrains internally funded growth and shareholder returns, while the gap between accounting profit and available cash is especially important given the company’s leverage.

Higher operating costs can absorb part of the benefit from pricing and occupancy gains, putting pressure on margins if increases persist. Because cruise demand is cyclical and the company is emerging from a recovery period, profitability and growth may remain more volatile across changing travel conditions.
